content: Plasmodium vivax malaria has a unique characteristic of a dormant liver stage, which can reactivate and cause relapses of the disease, contributing to ongoing transmission. Primaquine (PQ) is the standard treatment used to eliminate this liver stage, but it requires a 14-day regimen and poses a risk of hemolysis in individuals with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. Tafenoquine (TQ) is a newer alternative to PQ, offering the advantage of a single-dose treatment due to its longer half-life. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy of a single 300 mg dose of tafenoquine in preventing relapses of P. vivax malaria. A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, up to June 3, 2020. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included if they assessed tafenoquine for relapse prevention, regardless of whether participants were screened for G6PD deficiency. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were performed independently by multiple reviewers. Since distinguishing true relapses from reinfections is challenging in endemic areas, recurrence of infection was used as a proxy for relapse. Meta-analyses were conducted where appropriate, and the certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Three RCTs conducted in endemic areas met the inclusion criteria. All participants in these trials received chloroquine (CQ) to treat the blood-stage infection, and individuals who were pregnant or G6PD-deficient were excluded. Tafenoquine 300 mg single dose versus no treatment for relapse prevention: Two trials compared tafenoquine to no antihypnozoite treatment. Tafenoquine 300 mg as a single dose reduced P. vivax recurrences during a six-month follow-up period, although there was moderate uncertainty regarding the effect size (Risk Ratio [RR] 0.32, 95% Confidence Interval [CI] 0.12 to 0.88; 2 trials, 504 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Among individuals with normal G6PD status, tafenoquine likely caused little or no difference in the occurrence of any type of adverse events (2 trials, 504 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). However, there is very low-certainty evidence regarding whether tafenoquine increases the risk of serious adverse events. Across the two trials, 23 serious adverse events were reported in the tafenoquine groups, with the majority (15 events) involving a significant drop in hemoglobin levels (>3 g/dL or >30% reduction from baseline). Tafenoquine 300 mg single dose versus primaquine 15 mg/day for 14 days for relapse prevention: Three trials compared tafenoquine to primaquine. The results suggest that tafenoquine and primaquine are likely similarly effective in preventing recurrences (used as a proxy for relapse) over a six-month follow-up period (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.8 to 1.34; 3 trials, 747 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). In individuals with normal G6PD status, there was likely little or no difference in the occurrence of any type of adverse events between the two drugs (3 trials, 747 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). However, there is very low-certainty evidence regarding whether tafenoquine increases the risk of serious adverse events compared to primaquine. Among the serious adverse events reported in the tafenoquine groups, the most common was a decline in hemoglobin levels (19 out of 29 events). Other serious adverse events observed in the tafenoquine group, such as hepatitis E infection, limb abscess, pneumonia, and menorrhagia, were considered unlikely to be caused by the drug. Conclusions: A single 300 mg dose of tafenoquine is effective in preventing relapses of P. vivax malaria compared to no antihypnozoite treatment. When compared to primaquine, tafenoquine appears to have similar efficacy in preventing recurrences, with no significant difference in overall adverse events in non-pregnant adults without G6PD deficiency. However, the inability to distinguish true relapses from recurrences in the available studies introduces some uncertainty into these findings. Tafenoquine has not been tested in children or individuals with G6PD deficiency. Its single-dose regimen offers a significant practical advantage over the 14-day primaquine regimen, without an apparent increase in adverse events in the studied population.
